quick: Epilepsy 60-200 mg/day; status epilepticus 15-20 mg/kg IV loading
May take with or without food
Risk; teratogenic and neonatal withdrawal/bleeding - use only if essential
Caution; significant transfer to milk - monitor infant for sedation
Serum phenobarbital level, sedation, respiration, CBC, LFTs; Habit forming: Yes
summary: Phenobarbitone (phenobarbital) is a long-acting barbiturate used as an antiepileptic for generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures and status epilepticus, and as a sedative. It is FDA-approved and a Schedule IV controlled substance - HABIT FORMING with risk of tolerance, dependence and life-threatening withdrawal. It is a potent CYP enzyme inducer with many interactions and a long half-life; doses are tapered, never stopped abruptly.
indications: Treatment of generalised tonic-clonic and partial (focal) seizures
Neonatal seizures and (off-label) management of neonatal abstinence/jaundice per specialist use

dosage.n: Long half-life allows once-daily dosing; titrate to level/response

dosage.d: 15-20 mg/kg IV at <=60 mg/min (max rate; respiratory support ready)
dosage.n: Risk of respiratory depression/hypotension; monitor closely
Adjust to serum level and response

admin: May be taken with or without food; take at the same time daily
Parenteral: give IV slowly (<=60 mg/min) with airway/respiratory support available; full effect of IV dose may take up to 30 minutes - avoid re-dosing too soon
Never stop abruptly - taper gradually to avoid withdrawal seizures and life-threatening withdrawal
Controlled substance (Schedule IV) - store securely and dispense per regulations
moa: Phenobarbital binds the GABA-A receptor chloride channel and prolongs the duration of chloride channel opening, enhancing inhibitory GABAergic neurotransmission; at higher concentrations it also reduces excitatory glutamate responses. The net CNS depression raises the seizure threshold and limits seizure spread.

absolute: History of manifest or latent porphyria
Severe respiratory disease with dyspnoea or obstruction
relative: Acute or chronic pain (may mask/cause paradoxical excitation)

preg: Risk. Phenobarbital crosses the placenta and is associated with congenital malformations, neonatal coagulation defects (give vitamin K), and neonatal withdrawal. Use only if essential, at the lowest effective dose, with specialist supervision and folic acid supplementation.
lact: Phenobarbital is excreted into breast milk in significant amounts and can cause infant sedation and feeding difficulty; if used, monitor the infant closely for drowsiness and poor feeding.
renal: Excreted partly unchanged renally; reduce dose or extend the dosing interval in renal impairment and monitor levels. Alkalinisation of urine increases its elimination.
hepatic: Metabolised hepatically and contraindicated in marked hepatic impairment; in lesser impairment reduce the dose and monitor.

major: CNS depressants/opioids/benzodiazepines/alcohol - additive sedation and fatal respiratory depression

Strong CYP induction reduces levels/efficacy of warfarin, oral contraceptives (contraceptive failure), corticosteroids, doxycycline, theophylline, many antiepileptics, antiretrovirals, ciclosporin, etc.
Sodium valproate - inhibits phenobarbital metabolism, raising its level and toxicity
moderate: Other antiepileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine) - complex bidirectional changes; monitor levels
Antidepressants/antipsychotics - lowered seizure threshold and additive sedation
minor: Folic acid - may lower phenobarbital levels
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive CNS and respiratory depression that can be fatal.
interactions.diagnostics: Therapeutic drug monitoring used (target ~15-40 mcg/mL); induces hepatic enzymes affecting other drug levels.

serious: Physical dependence and severe withdrawal (seizures, delirium)
rare: Osteomalacia/reduced bone density with long use

monitoring: Respiratory rate and sedation, especially parenteral and with other depressants
CBC, liver and renal function periodically
Mood and suicidal ideation; signs of dependence/withdrawal
Bone health and vitamin D with long-term use
counsel: This medicine can be habit forming - take exactly as prescribed and never stop suddenly
Do not drink alcohol or take other sedatives/opioids without medical advice - the combination can stop your breathing
It may make you drowsy - do not drive until you know how it affects you
It can make hormonal contraception fail - use an additional method
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, and report rash, mood changes or thoughts of self-harm
pk: Oral ~30-60 min; IV onset within minutes but peak brain effect up to ~30 min
Store at 20-25 C, protected from light; secure as a controlled substance
pearls: Habit forming: Yes - Schedule IV controlled substance with tolerance, dependence and dangerous withdrawal
Potent CYP enzyme inducer - causes oral contraceptive failure and lowers many drug levels
Never withdraw abruptly; taper to avoid rebound/status epilepticus
Very long half-life - steady state takes 2-3 weeks; once-daily dosing is feasible
Contraindicated in porphyria and marked hepatic impairment; give neonatal vitamin K if used in pregnancy
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one - do not double up. Because of the long half-life and dependence risk, do not stop the medicine on your own.
overdose: Overdose causes CNS depression progressing to coma, respiratory depression, hypotension, hypothermia and absent reflexes; it can be fatal. There is no specific antidote - give supportive intensive care with airway/ventilatory support, fluids/vasopressors, activated charcoal, urinary alkalinisation to enhance elimination, and haemodialysis/haemoperfusion in severe poisoning.
